youtube_title: Money Sent by Mistake — and the Recipients Got to Keep It (This Time)
caption: Australia's High Court (2014) let Hills and Bosch keep payments made to them by mistake because, in good faith, they had given up pursuing real debts in reliance on them. Not a license to spend a windfall.
script: A company got money sent to them by mistake, and Australia's highest court said, keep it. [disclaimer] Meet a businessman in Australia. He's running a scam. He makes fake bills for equipment from two real suppliers, Hills Industries and Bosch. A finance company pays those suppliers. Then it finds out the bills were fake. The finance company wants its money back. Normally, if someone pays you by mistake, you have to give it back. But Hills and Bosch had no idea about the scam. They thought the money was payment for real debts the business owed them. So they stopped chasing those debts. And they kept doing business with that group. Wait. In twenty fourteen, every judge on Australia's top court says they can keep it? You see, the question was whether keeping it would be unfair. They gave up real debts because of that money. It's like trading your bike for a car, and then being told to give back the car, but not get back the bike. This only works if you acted in good faith and truly gave something up. Random money in your account that you spend? You can still be forced to pay it back. So the scammer's fake bills ended up paying off his real debts. [loop] So if money ever lands in your account by mistake, remember

script_old: Someone sent money by mistake, and the companies that received it won the right to keep it, in this particular case. This is Australia's High Court, in twenty fourteen. A finance company, AFSL, was tricked by a fraud. A director in a business group created false invoices for equipment from two suppliers, Hills Industries and Bosch Security Systems. AFSL paid those suppliers, then discovered the invoices were fake, and wanted its money back. Normally, money paid by mistake can be recovered. But Hills and Bosch weren't in on the fraud. When the money arrived, they treated it as payment of real debts the business group owed them. They stopped chasing those debts, and they kept trading with the group. They had changed their position because of that money. The High Court unanimously said they didn't have to repay. The test was whether keeping the money would be inequitable in all the circumstances, and given what they'd given up, it wasn't. Here's the limit. This defense depends on good faith, and on genuinely changing your position because of the payment. If a surprise deposit hits your account and you rush out to spend it, that's not this case, and you can still be made to pay it back. [loop] So if money ever lands in your account by mistake, remember
